question.text: What did the Entscheidungsproblem ask for?

prove-every-formula.text: A proof of every formula of logic
prove-every-formula.why: Many formulas cannot be proved. The question asked for a method that tells which ones can.

fast-computer.why: The question is about methods. Speed plays no part in it.

decide-provable.text: A method that decides, for every formula, whether it is provable
decide-provable.why: That is the question, as Turing states it. The method must work for every formula and always stop.

list-of-proofs.text: A machine lists every provable formula, one after another. Why does this not answer the question?

never-says-no.text: For a formula that is not provable, the machine never says “no”
never-says-no.why: That formula never appears in the list, so the machine runs forever.

misses-some.text: The list misses some provable formulas
misses-some.why: Every provable formula appears in the list sooner or later. The problem is the other formulas.

too-long.text: The list is too long to print
too-long.why: Length is not the problem. The machine never stops for a formula that is not provable.

un-m.text: What does Turing’s formula Un(ℳ) mean?

stops.why: Turing’s route does not use stopping. It uses “ever prints 0”, as in lesson 4.

zero-on-tape.text: That at some moment, the figure 0 is on the tape of ℳ
zero-on-tape.why: Turing gives this meaning on page 260. He writes the figure 0 as S1.

circle-free.why: Section 11 uses the second result of section 8, “ever prints 0”, not circle-free machines.

route.text: Assume that a machine decides, for every formula, whether it is provable. What follows?

every-formula-provable.why: A decision does not change which formulas are provable. It only tells which ones are.

nothing.text: Nothing, because logic and machines are separate subjects
nothing.why: Un(ℳ) links them. It turns a question about a machine into a question about a formula.

decides-zero.text: A machine could decide whether any machine ever prints 0, which is impossible
decides-zero.why: Give it Un(ℳ). Its answer says whether ℳ ever prints 0, and lesson 4 showed that no machine can decide that.

church.text: Who else answered the Entscheidungsproblem in 1936?

hilbert.text: Hilbert, with a method for every formula
hilbert.why: Hilbert and Ackermann asked the question. The answer, no, came from Church and Turing.

church.text: Church, with his own idea of what is “effectively calculable”
church.why: His answer is a short note in the Journal of Symbolic Logic. Turing cites it on page 231.

nobody.text: Nobody: Turing was the only one
nobody.why: Church answered too, in a short note. Turing’s paper cites it on page 231.
